note: Original reading prompts and brief factual notes. Theme paths are editorial suggestions, not claims about an author's intent.

Emma Lazarus.bio: Emma Lazarus (1849–1887) was an American poet. The New Colossus was written in 1883 for a fundraiser for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal.

William Blake.bio: William Blake (1757–1827) was an English poet, printmaker and painter. Songs of Innocence and of Experience combines poems with his own illustrations.

Emily Dickinson.bio: Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) lived in Amherst, Massachusetts. Most of her poems appeared in print after her death; early editions sometimes altered punctuation and wording.

Cyprian Kamil Norwid.bio: Cyprian Norwid (1821–1883) was a Polish poet and artist who spent much of his adult life abroad. This reader uses his original Polish text, not a modern translation.

Walt Whitman.bio: Walt Whitman (1819–1892) was an American poet. He revised and expanded Leaves of Grass across several editions during his lifetime.

William Wordsworth.bio: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) was an English Romantic poet. He published Lyrical Ballads with Samuel Taylor Coleridge in 1798.

Paul Laurence Dunbar.bio: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906) was an American poet, novelist and short-story writer. His poetry uses both standard English and dialect.

Elizabeth Barrett Browning.bio: Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1806–1861) was an English poet. Her publications include Sonnets from the Portuguese and the verse novel Aurora Leigh.

Eugenio Montale.bio: Eugenio Montale (1896–1981) was an Italian poet and the 1975 Nobel laureate in literature. His work appears here as a reading reference, with no protected verse reproduced.

Ryszard Krynicki.bio: Ryszard Krynicki is a Polish poet and translator. Magnetic Point is a selection of his poems published in English by New Directions.

Camillo Sbarbaro.bio: Camillo Sbarbaro (1888–1967) was an Italian poet. Pianissimo is one of his poetry collections; the reader links to an authorized reading source.

Karol Wojtyła (John Paul II).bio: Karol Wojtyła (1920–2005), later Pope John Paul II, wrote poetry and plays. His work appears here as reading references only.

prompts: Which image do you remember after the last line? Return to that line.
Read once to the punctuation, then once to the line endings. What changes?
Where does the voice change direction? Look for a verb or a small linking word.
Which sound repeats? Follow it through a second reading.
What is left unsaid? Distinguish your inference from the words on the page.
Try reading it as a letter to one person. Does the voice change?
Where do you agree with the speaker, and where do you resist?
Read the first line, then the last. What has moved between them?
Find one concrete object. What would be lost if it disappeared?
Choose a line to read aloud twice, once quickly and once slowly.
